debate.situation: You are the one who always initiates plans with a friend. In person it is lovely, but when you stop texting, contact stops, and you are wondering whether to bring it up. What you know is the pattern; what you do not know is why it exists (low-initiator habits, busyness, a lopsided friendship, or something else) or how much the imbalance matters to you.

minds.title: The Friendship Idealist
minds.concern: Friendship should be freely given, not audited; scorekeeping can poison the thing you are trying to protect.
minds.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

minds.title: The Conversation Clarifier
minds.concern: Facts, stories and feelings get tangled; say what you observed, own your part, and ask rather than assume.
minds.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen

minds.title: The Friendship Realist
minds.concern: Friendships decay without regular contact, people differ in how they keep them up, and effort is a limited resource.
minds.author: Robin Dunbar
minds.book: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: Say nothing. If you start counting who texted last, you have turned a friend into a ledger. The evenings are lovely, so that is the friendship. A confrontation about texting risks making a warm thing feel like a performance review.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Emerson, Essays: First Series, the essay on Friendship (paraphrase; link not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: But the ledger is already running, just in your head. Friendships fade without contact, and someone has to supply it. If you carry all of it silently, resentment is the likely outcome, and that damages the lovely evenings more than one honest remark would.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
debate.basis: Basis: Dunbar, How Many Friends Does One Person Need?, on friendships decaying without contact (paraphrase; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: Resentment is a risk, I grant. But notice you are assuming the silence means something. Maybe your friend simply likes being invited. If I pressed her for equal effort, I would be demanding proof of love in a currency she may not use.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Emerson, Essays: First Series, the essay on Friendship (paraphrase; link not verified)

debate.speaker: The Conversation Clarifier
debate.text: Exactly: that is a story, and so is the resentment one. What you observed is narrow: you plan, she meets you warmly, and contact stops when you stop. Why is unknown. A good opening reports that and asks about it, instead of arguing a verdict.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on separating what happened from the story we tell about it (paraphrase; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: I will push back on asking at all. People differ a lot in how they maintain friends. Some only ever show up in person. A direct question can make her feel accused of failing at something she never knew was a test.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
debate.basis: Basis: Dunbar, How Many Friends Does One Person Need?, on individual differences in maintaining friendships (paraphrase; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Conversation Clarifier
debate.text: Fair, so the framing matters more than the decision. Accusing is one thing. Saying that you love your time together, that you have noticed you usually start the plans, and that you are curious how she sees it, is another. It invites her view.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on opening with a shared purpose and curiosity (paraphrase; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: Now I am uneasy about the word curious. A planned talk about the pattern still announces that something is wrong. I would rather you test it quietly: stop initiating for a few weeks and see what freedom reveals, with no accusation attached.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Emerson, Essays: First Series, the essay on Friendship (paraphrase; link not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: That experiment has a cost I would flag. If she is simply a low initiator, you may lose a good friend to a silence that proved nothing. I would go further than Dunbar here: set a limit in advance, a few weeks, and decide what you will do with the result.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
debate.basis: Basis: Dunbar, How Many Friends Does One Person Need?, on friendships decaying without contact (paraphrase; the added limit is my own extension; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Conversation Clarifier
debate.text: And a silent test is its own story-making. You will read her quiet as an answer, when it might be habit. Conceding the Idealist's point, I would hold the conversation back until you have either tried a gentle, low-stakes ask or know that the imbalance truly bothers you.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on the stories we build from limited information (paraphrase; source not verified)

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: I can accept that. If it truly bothers you, silence is not generosity, it is a slow leak. My remaining disagreement is tone: keep it light enough that she can answer honestly, not defensively. A friend who feels free will say more.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Emerson, Essays: First Series, the essay on Friendship (paraphrase; link not verified)

debate.clearer: The debate narrowed from whether to speak to what you would be speaking about. What you actually observed (you start the plans, contact lapses when you stop, the meetings are warm) does not yet tell you why. The minds still disagree on whether a spoken conversation or a quiet, time-limited experiment is the gentler first step, and on how much effort a friendship should be expected to take. One possible reflection: is the imbalance something that bothers you now, or something you expect might bother you later?
debate.dependsOn: If the imbalance bothers you and the friendship matters to you, a light, non-accusing remark that reports what you noticed and asks for her view becomes more reasonable, because it lets her answer before resentment builds. If it does not bother you much, and the warmth when you meet is enough, doing nothing is reasonable, because you are choosing the friendship as it is rather than the one you imagined. If you suspect she is a low initiator rather than uninterested, a small, specific ask (for example, inviting her to suggest the next plan) may work better than a talk about the pattern. If you are unsure why she is quiet, a time-limited pause in your initiating, with a date to reassess, is a proportionate way to learn more, though silence alone will not tell you her reasons.
